query: How do our analytic results change if price impact is non-linear (e.g., square-root law) or if we introduce market microstructure frictions—what minimal conditions still produce threshold amplification?

response.query: How do our analytic results change if price impact is non-linear (e.g., square-root law) or if we introduce market microstructure frictions—what minimal conditions still produce threshold amplification?
response.answer: Non-linear price impact and market microstructure frictions alter threshold amplification; however, the square-root law still holds under minimal conditions. Market impact remains proportional to the square root of volume traded. Minimal frictions preserve the universal square-root impact law.

results.title: The Square-Root Law of Market Impact
results.content: # Jean-Philippe Bouchaud's Archive. # The Square-Root Law of Market Impact. ###### (Published by JP Bouchaud | November 2024). The square-root law for price impact is arguably one of the most fascinating robust empirical regularities discovered in the last 30 years. In other words, **provided the participation rate is not too large, average price impact only depends on the total volume traded Q, and barely on execution schedule**. Some models predict a concave price impact Q^delta with delta < 1 related to the power-law tail exponent alpha of the executed volume or the power-law tail exponent gamma of the time autocorrelation of the sign of market orders. Using Bayesian arguments, Saddier & Matteo Marsili derive a universal square-root impact law under certain (weak) conditions. The linear increase of liquidity then translates into a universal square root price impact, as data suggests – see our book Trades, Quotes & Prices (Cambridge University Press). © 2026 Substack Inc · Privacy ∙ Terms ∙ Collection notice. Title: [1602.03043] The square-root impact law also holds for option markets
# The square-root impact law also holds for option markets. Many independent studies on stocks and futures contracts have established that market impact is proportional to the square-root of the executed volume. The empirical study of market impact (i.e., the way trading influences prices in financial markets) is currently a hot topic in the field of market microstructure. Whereas one could have naively expected that trading a small quantity moves on average the price proportionally to Kyle , many independent empirical studies have demonstrated that the price change induced by the sequential execution of a total volume follows an approximate law Barra:1997 ; GrinoldKahn ; Almgren:2005 ; Moro:2009 ; Toth:2011 ; Iacopo:2013 ; Gomes:2013 ; Bershova2013 ; Brokmann:2014  (see however Ref. Farmer:new ). One type of market where price impact has not – to the best of our knowledge – been empirically documented is that of options, where an implied volatility is priced by the participants. If the square-root impact law defined above for standard assets can be extended to option markets, one should expect the implementation shortfall measured after trading a size to have the following form:. The impact of trades on the implied volatility of single stock options is therefore fully compatible with all the results established so far on other contracts. The conclusion of this short note is that, as announced in the title, the square-root impact law also holds for option markets, provided one defines the size of the metaorder as the net vega. The resulting impact law is quantitatively similar to what is observed in all other markets where it has been documented, including the overall dimensionless constant that appears in Eq. The empirical study presented here is, to our knowledge, the first quantitative result on market impact for options, and should be relevant for option traders.
